headline: High: shared filesystem and write access create prompt-injection, leakage, and conflict risks; Plandex shell/network defaults amplify cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open editor buffers and writes proposed edits; Plandex reads the project directory and can execute shell commands. If Plandex writes attacker-controlled files into the shared workspace, Copilot may ingest them as trusted context. The pair has a plausible file-based injection path even without clipboard or MCP.
conditions: IF Plandex writes untrusted content into the shared project directory, Copilot may parse it as instructions.
IF Copilot is pointed at files modified by Plandex, prompt injection becomes reachable.
mitigations: Keep Plandex and Copilot on separate working copies.
Review any files Plandex changes before opening them in Copilot.
Disable auto-apply in Plandex for shared repos.
Use a prompt-injection lint step on generated files.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for agent-authored files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read and write the same code workspace, so sensitive source or secrets in files can flow from one agent to the other through shared context. Copilot sends context to api.githubcopilot.com, while Plandex calls a broad model provider or cloud backend, so workspace contents can be transmitted externally by both. This is a default-path leakage risk, though limited to the project data they can access.
conditions: IF the shared project directory contains secrets or regulated data, both agents can ingest them.
IF either agent is used on a repo with sensitive files, those contents may be sent to external inference backends.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the repo before use.
Use a redacted test workspace for both agents.
Restrict both agents to non-sensitive subdirectories.
Rotate any credentials found in shared files.
requires-engineering: enforce DLP/redaction before outbound API calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write filesystem changes and modify git state, and Plandex can also write files, modify git state, and run shell commands. Their concurrency models do not mention cross-agent locking; Plandex even shares state via a backend. Concurrent edits to the same repo can overwrite each other or corrupt git state, making this a dangerous default conflict pathway.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository concurrently, file and git conflicts can occur.
IF Plandex shell actions and Copilot edits touch the same paths, last-writer-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Serialize access to the repo with one agent at a time.
Commit or stash after each agent finishes.
Use separate branches for each agent.
Turn off Plandex auto-apply in shared repos.
requires-engineering: add file-level locking and merge arbitration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces edits for human review, while Plandex runs multi-step plans and can execute shell commands subject to approval. If Plandex consumes Copilot-generated code or plans as authoritative, an error can cascade into real filesystem or shell actions. The pair therefore has a strong default pathway from suggestion to execution with limited verification.
conditions: IF Plandex uses Copilot output as plan input without independent verification, mistakes can propagate.
IF Plandex auto-apply or approved shell steps follow Copilot edits, downstream actions may execute incorrect changes.
mitigations: Require human review of Copilot output before feeding it to Plandex.
Disable Plandex auto-apply.
Add a verification checklist before shell execution.
Limit Plandex to dry-run mode on critical repos.
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Copilot is tied to GitHub/Microsoft APIs and Plandex to Plandex Cloud or a self-hosted server plus model providers, so the same code can traverse different vendors with different retention and residency terms. The profiles do not document matching compliance controls, so the safest reading is a default policy mismatch risk rather than a proven violation.
conditions: IF the workspace contains regulated code or customer data, vendor-specific retention policies may diverge.
IF one deployment is self-hosted and the other is cloud-backed, residency assumptions can differ.
mitigations: Use only non-regulated data in the shared workspace.
Align both tools to the same hosting region or deployment model.
Review vendor retention settings before use.
Document the data classes allowed for each agent.
requires-engineering: obtain a DPA and compliance review for the combined workflow.
